tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__get_meeting_transcript
tools.description: Get the verbatim transcript of a Granola meeting by ID; no summaries or notes. Returns up to 40000 characters per call by default (max_chars, up to 80000), cut at an utterance boundary with total_chars, truncated and next_offset reported. A page that splits an oversized utterance has ends_mid_utterance and the next starts_mid_utterance. With meeting_ids, meetings has one entry per requested ID in request order, with the single-read fields or an error. The batch shares 80000 characters: each meeting returns up to max_chars or an equal share of that, whichever is smaller. Pass offsets to continue several meetings in one call. An accessible meeting with no transcript returns transcript null (status "unavailable" for chunk reads) and transcript_unavailable with a reason: transcript_pending means retry in a few minutes; not_happened_yet means retry after the meeting; no_transcript and transcript_deleted are final. "Meeting not found" means the ID does not resolve or is not accessible. Transcript blocks separate audio source (Microphone/System audio) from speaker identity; mobile/imported transcripts may keep Speaker A/B labels. For native recordings, recording context identifies the document owner as the recorder, not necessarily the speaker; missing recorder data stays unknown. Needs a paid Granola plan. If it returns a paid-plan error, use the other meeting tools and say when their results lack the requested detail.

schema.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__get_meeting_transcript
schema.description: Get the verbatim transcript of a Granola meeting by ID; no summaries or notes. Returns up to 40000 characters per call by default (max_chars, up to 80000), cut at an utterance boundary with total_chars, truncated and next_offset reported. A page that splits an oversized utterance has ends_mid_utterance and the next starts_mid_utterance. With meeting_ids, meetings has one entry per requested ID in request order, with the single-read fields or an error. The batch shares 80000 characters: each meeting returns up to max_chars or an equal share of that, whichever is smaller. Pass offsets to continue several meetings in one call. An accessible meeting with no transcript returns transcript null (status "unavailable" for chunk reads) and transcript_unavailable with a reason: transcript_pending means retry in a few minutes; not_happened_yet means retry after the meeting; no_transcript and transcript_deleted are final. "Meeting not found" means the ID does not resolve or is not accessible. Transcript blocks separate audio source (Microphone/System audio) from speaker identity; mobile/imported transcripts may keep Speaker A/B labels. For native recordings, recording context identifies the document owner as the recorder, not necessarily the speaker; missing recorder data stays unknown. Needs a paid Granola plan. If it returns a paid-plan error, use the other meeting tools and say when their results lack the requested detail.

meeting_ids.description: Meeting UUIDs or public note IDs (max 10). With several IDs, offset applies to each meeting and the meetings share 80000 characters, so each returns up to max_chars or an equal share, whichever is smaller; use offsets to start meetings at different positions. A meeting that cannot be read gets an error entry and the others are still returned. Empty arrays are ignored.

note_ids.description: Alias for meeting_ids. If both are nonempty, they must refer to the same set of notes; order, duplicates, and UUID/public ID format may differ.

meeting_id.description: Alias for meeting_ids with a single meeting. Every ID argument provided must name the same meetings.

note_id.description: Alias for meeting_ids with a single meeting. Every ID argument provided must name the same meetings.

offset.description: Character offset; pass next_offset to continue, with the same include_timestamps as that page.

max_chars.description: Maximum size of the transcript field as sent (integer, at least 1,000), cut at the last utterance that fits; a page holds fewer transcript characters when the text needs JSON escaping. Defaults to 40000; larger requests are capped at 80000. Use next_offset to continue. Lower it if responses exceed your output limit.

include_timestamps.description: Prefix each reliably timed block with [m:ss], minutes:seconds since the transcript's earliest timed block, not clock time; that block can predate the meeting when recording started early. Applies to every page; chunk_ids reads always include them. Adds about 7 characters per block, and offset, next_offset and total_chars count the text as rendered with it, so keep the same value when continuing from next_offset. When no block has timing, no prefixes are added and timestamps_unavailable says so.

offsets.description: With meeting_ids only: character offset per meeting, keyed by meeting ID, e.g. {"<id>": 8000}. Pass each truncated meeting's next_offset to continue several transcripts in one call. Meetings not listed start at offset. Omit or pass {} when not needed.

chunk_ids.description: Read up to ten finalized transcript chunks instead of the full transcript. Use chunk IDs from search_transcripts, or [0] to browse from the beginning. IDs past the last chunk are skipped and listed in ignored_chunk_ids; if none of the IDs exist the status is out_of_range. Each chunk's transcript is verbatim text in the full read's format: one block per speaker turn, prefixed with [m:ss] (minutes:seconds since the transcript's earliest timed block, omitted when unknown) and the speaker label; preformatted transcripts keep their own text and labels. Also returns total_chunks and previous/next chunk IDs.

transcript_version.description: With chunk_ids, reuse the version from search or a previous chunk read. A changed status returns no chunks: search again or restart browsing without the old version. Omit chunk_ids and transcript_version for the existing full transcript read.

tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__get_meetings
tools.description: Read one or more Granola meetings by ID: private notes, AI summary, attendees, metadata and note URLs. Use it when you have meeting IDs from discovery results or note URLs; batch up to 10 IDs per call. Private notes appear only for meetings the user owns (status "empty": no text; "not_included": another user owns the note). meeting_at is the calendar event's scheduled start (created_at without an event), so it can differ from when the meeting was recorded. Invalid, missing and inaccessible IDs are reported separately; the other meetings are still returned. If the meetings would exceed 80000 characters, the last ones are left out and listed in omitted_meetings; read them in another call. The first meeting is always returned whole, so one long meeting can exceed 80000 characters. The note creator and participants are not necessarily the connected user: confirm the connected user's identity with get_account_info and match it to explicit ownership evidence before drafting in the user's voice or assigning them actions; first-person notes are not proof of the user's voice. Dated plans do not establish current progress. known_participants comes from the calendar invite, attendees added by hand, and the note creator; anyone else who spoke appears only in the notes and transcript. Does not return transcripts; notes can omit details that were discussed. If a detail is missing, get_meeting_transcript may have it on a paid Granola plan; if it returns a paid-plan error, say the detail is missing rather than conclude it was never discussed. Shared-screen screenshots appear in <attachments> with an ID, time offset and lossy description; for anything visual (designs, slides, charts, code), view them with get_meeting_attachment. Attached photos appear as <attachment type="photo"> without a description; view them with get_meeting_attachment. Keep at most 5 get_meetings calls in flight, and only for calls you already need. On a rate_limit error, retry only the failed call after retry_after_seconds, one at a time, and not when retryable is false.

tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__search_meetings
tools.description: Find the user's meetings by keyword, participant/company, date, or a combination. Keyword searches cover meeting titles, summaries and your private notes. They do not search transcripts: an empty result does not mean a term was never spoken in a meeting. Returns metadata only (title, date, participants, note headings), not what was said: read the relevant meetings with get_meetings before answering about their content, and use get_meetings directly for a meeting you already identified. With keywords or participant, results are ranked by relevance favouring recent meetings; with neither, newest first, defaulting to the last 7 days unless folder_id is set. Pages can be short or empty; continue with next_cursor while it is present. completion_status incomplete means continuation is unavailable: narrow the search. participant matches participant metadata (names, emails, companies, domains), not mentions in notes, as an AND filter with the other inputs; metadata can be incomplete. For broader questions about a person or company, also search their name plus the topic in keywords with participant omitted: internal discussions may hold the answer. Captures of the same calendar event are grouped, keeping the user's own note or else the newest; read other_ids in duplicate_recordings only for details the listed note lacks or when the user asks to compare attendees' notes. Use attended_only=true for 'my meetings'. list_meeting_folders gives folder_id values. Keyword matching is literal, so pass the user's words plus obvious synonyms. Meetings with viewable attachments carry an attachment_count attribute; get_meetings lists them. Keep at most 2 search_meetings calls in flight, and only for calls you already need. folder_id.description: Only return meetings in this folder or its nested folders. Use list_meeting_folders to discover folder IDs.

workspace_only.description: Set to true only when the user explicitly asks for Team Space, public workspace, or workspace-visible meetings. Omit or set to false to search every meeting the user is allowed to access. Combines with folder_id and include_shared using AND.

keywords.description: Groups of words to search for in meeting titles, summaries, or your private notes. Transcript text is not searched. from_date.description: Only meetings on or after this ISO date or time, using calendar start when available, otherwise note creation. to_date.description: Only meetings on or before this ISO date or time. YYYY-MM-DD includes the whole day in the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable); explicit offsets are respected. Uses calendar start when available, otherwise note creation.

tools.description:

tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

=== README.md
     1	# Subvox
     2	
     3	A macOS prototype that tests whether AirPods Pro head-motion data (`CMHeadphoneMotionManager`) carries enough information to turn **silently mouthed words into text**.
     4	
     5	It doesn't use a language model. It's a small-vocabulary template recognizer plus a statistical test that tells you whether the signal is real.
     6	
     7	## Build & run
     8	
     9	```sh
    10	brew install xcodegen   # once
    11	xcodegen generate
    12	open Subvox.xcodeproj   # ⌘R
    13	```
    14	
    15	Or from the command line:
    16	
    17	```sh
    18	xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build -allowProvisioningUpdates build
    19	open build/Build/Products/Debug/Subvox.app
    20	xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build test
    21	```
    22	
    23	Requires macOS 14+, AirPods Pro or another headphone that supports head tracking, connected as the Mac's audio output. On first launch, grant **Motion**. The mic and speech prompts only appear when you start the mic.
    24	
    25	## Screens
    26	
    27	| Screen | What it does |
    28	|---|---|
    29	| **Sensors** | Live plots of user acceleration, rotation rate and attitude, the measured sample rate, a mic input picker and level meter, and a recorder for experiment sessions. |
    30	| **Train** | Pick a word, hold **Space**, mouth it, release. Each take is stored as a template. **Evaluate** runs leave-one-out classification and a 500× label-permutation test, then shows accuracy against chance, a p-value and a confusion matrix. The feature checkboxes (acceleration / rotation / attitude) let you test which channels carry the signal. |
    31	| **Decode** | The motion-to-text screen. Hold Space, or use auto-detect after calibrating the noise floor. Each segment is DTW-matched against your templates and added to the transcript. A live mic transcript runs alongside it for comparison. |
    32	
    33	## How decoding works
    34	
    35	1. **Segmentation** (`CaptureController`). Space-hold, or an energy trigger above a calibrated noise floor with pre-roll and hangover.
    36	2. **Features** (`MotionFeatures`). Per frame: user acceleration (3), rotation rate (3), and attitude change since the start of the segment (3). Each channel is mean-centered, and quiet lead-in and lead-out frames are trimmed.
    37	3. **Matching** (`DTW`, `TemplateClassifier`). Each channel is z-scaled across the training set. Matching is 1-nearest-neighbour per word, using dynamic time warping with a Sakoe–Chiba band. A segment is rejected if the best distance is above *max distance* or the margin to the runner-up is below *min confidence*.
    38	4. **Is it real?** (`Evaluation`). The leave-one-out accuracy is compared with the same procedure run on shuffled labels. If p < 0.05, the motion stream distinguishes your words better than chance.
    39	
    40	## Experiment protocol
    41	
    42	Use **Record Session** in the toolbar or on the Sensors screen. Recordings go to `~/Documents/Subvox/Sessions/<timestamp>-<condition>/`:
    43	
    44	- `motion.csv`: every motion sample. `t` is seconds from session start.
    45	- `audio.caf`: microphone audio, if the mic is running.
    46	- `events.csv`: every Space-held segment, with its label or prediction.
    47	- `meta.json`: condition, prompt, and the audio start offset for aligning audio with motion.
    48	
    49	Suggested runs: the same 5-word script under **Normal speech**, **Whisper** and **Silent mouthing**, 10 reps each. Then, in Train, compare the Evaluate results across feature sets.
    50	
    51	The training set lives at `~/Library/Application Support/Subvox/dataset.json`.
    52	
    53	## Known limits
    54	
    55	- Headphone motion is processed and low-rate (roughly 25 Hz on AirPods). The speech-detecting accelerometer and the inward mic are not exposed. Expect jaw and head movement, not vocal vibration.
    56	- Templates are user- and session-specific. Re-seating the AirPods can shift the signal.
    57	- Choosing AirPods as the mic input switches them to the Bluetooth headset (HFP) profile.

     1	import Foundation
     2	
     3	/// Dynamic time warping between two multichannel sequences, with a Sakoe–Chiba band.
     4	/// Lets the same mouthed word match when said faster or slower.
     5	enum DTW {
     6	    static func distance(_ a: [[Double]], _ b: [[Double]], bandFraction: Double = 0.25) -> Double {
     7	        let n = a.count, m = b.count
     8	        guard n > 0, m > 0 else { return .infinity }
     9	        let band = max(abs(n - m), Int(Double(max(n, m)) * bandFraction))
    10	
    11	        var previous = [Double](repeating: .infinity, count: m + 1)
    12	        var current = previous
    13	        previous[0] = 0
    14	
    15	        for i in 1...n {
    16	            for j in current.indices { current[j] = .infinity }
    17	            let lo = max(1, i - band)
    18	            let hi = min(m, i + band)
    19	            if lo <= hi {
    20	                for j in lo...hi {
    21	                    let cost = euclidean(a[i - 1], b[j - 1])
    22	                    current[j] = cost + min(previous[j], current[j - 1], previous[j - 1])
    23	                }
    24	            }
    25	            swap(&previous, &current)
    26	        }
    27	        // Normalize by the maximum path length so long and short words compare fairly.
    28	        return previous[m] / Double(n + m)
    29	    }
    30	
    31	    private static func euclidean(_ x: [Double], _ y: [Double]) -> Double {
    32	        var sum = 0.0
    33	        for k in 0..<min(x.count, y.count) {
    34	            let d = x[k] - y[k]
    35	            sum += d * d
    36	        }
    37	        return sum.squareRoot()
    38	    }
    39	}

    14	enum MotionFeatures {
    15	    /// Activity score used for segmentation. Rotation (rad/s) and acceleration (g) live on
    16	    /// different scales; the 5× weight puts typical jaw-motion values in the same range.
    17	    static func energy(_ s: MotionSample) -> Double {
    18	        let rotation = (s.rx * s.rx + s.ry * s.ry + s.rz * s.rz).squareRoot()
    19	        let accel = (s.ax * s.ax + s.ay * s.ay + s.az * s.az).squareRoot()
    20	        return rotation + 5 * accel
    21	    }
    22	
    23	    /// Drops quiet lead-in/lead-out frames so templates align on the articulation itself.
    24	    /// Uses a threshold relative to the segment so it behaves the same for training and decoding.
    25	    static func trim(_ samples: [MotionSample], padding: Int = 2) -> [MotionSample] {
    26	        guard samples.count > 6 else { return samples }
    27	        let energies = samples.map(energy)
    28	        let sorted = energies.sorted()
    29	        let floor = sorted[sorted.count / 5]
    30	        let peak = sorted[sorted.count - 1]
    31	        guard peak > floor * 1.5 else { return samples }
    32	        let threshold = floor + 0.15 * (peak - floor)
    33	        guard let first = energies.firstIndex(where: { $0 > threshold }),
    34	              let last = energies.lastIndex(where: { $0 > threshold }) else { return samples }
    35	        let lo = max(0, first - padding)
    36	        let hi = min(samples.count - 1, last + padding)
    37	        guard hi - lo + 1 >= 5 else { return samples }
    38	        return Array(samples[lo...hi])
    39	    }

    41	    /// Per-frame feature vectors, mean-centered per channel (removes posture/heading bias).
    42	    static func frames(_ samples: [MotionSample], set: FeatureSet) -> [[Double]] {
    43	        guard let origin = samples.first else { return [] }
    44	        var frames = samples.map { s -> [Double] in
    45	            var v: [Double] = []
    46	            if set.contains(.acceleration) { v += [s.ax, s.ay, s.az] }
    47	            if set.contains(.rotation) { v += [s.rx, s.ry, s.rz] }
    48	            if set.contains(.attitude) {
    49	                v += [wrapped(s.pitch - origin.pitch), wrapped(s.roll - origin.roll), wrapped(s.yaw - origin.yaw)]
    50	            }
    51	            return v
    52	        }
    53	        guard let dims = frames.first?.count, dims > 0 else { return frames }
    54	        for d in 0..<dims {
    55	            let mean = frames.reduce(0) { $0 + $1[d] } / Double(frames.count)

    62	    static func channelScales(_ sequences: [[[Double]]]) -> [Double] {
    63	        guard let dims = sequences.first?.first?.count else { return [] }
    64	        var sum = [Double](repeating: 0, count: dims)
    65	        var sumSq = [Double](repeating: 0, count: dims)

    67	        for sequence in sequences {

4	     3	A macOS prototype that tests whether AirPods Pro head-motion data (`CMHeadphoneMotionManager`) carries enough information to turn **silently mouthed words into text**.
5	     4	
6	     5	It doesn't use a language model. It's a small-vocabulary template recognizer plus a statistical test that tells you whether the signal is real.
7	     6	
8	     7	## Build & run
9	     8	
10	     9	```sh
11	    10	brew install xcodegen   # once
12	    11	xcodegen generate
13	    12	open Subvox.xcodeproj   # ⌘R
14	    13	```
15	    14	
16	    15	Or from the command line:
17	    16	
18	    17	```sh
19	    18	xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build -allowProvisioningUpdates build
20	    19	open build/Build/Products/Debug/Subvox.app
21	    20	xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build test
22	    21	```
23	    22	
24	    23	Requires macOS 14+, AirPods Pro or another headphone that supports head tracking, connected as the Mac's audio output. On first launch, grant **Motion**. The mic and speech prompts only appear when you start the mic.
25	    24	
26	    25	## Screens
27	    26	
28	    27	| Screen | What it does |
29	    28	|---|---|
30	    29	| **Sensors** | Live plots of user acceleration, rotation rate and attitude, the measured sample rate, a mic input picker and level meter, and a recorder for experiment sessions. |
31	    30	| **Train** | Pick a word, hold **Space**, mouth it, release. Each take is stored as a template. **Evaluate** runs leave-one-out classification and a 500× label-permutation test, then shows accuracy against chance, a p-value and a confusion matrix. The feature checkboxes (acceleration / rotation / attitude) let you test which channels carry the signal. |
32	    31	| **Decode** | The motion-to-text screen. Hold Space, or use auto-detect after calibrating the noise floor. Each segment is DTW-matched against your templates and added to the transcript. A live mic transcript runs alongside it for comparison. |
33	    32	
34	    33	## How decoding works
35	    34	
36	    35	1. **Segmentation** (`CaptureController`). Space-hold, or an energy trigger above a calibrated noise floor with pre-roll and hangover.
37	    36	2. **Features** (`MotionFeatures`). Per frame: user acceleration (3), rotation rate (3), and attitude change since the start of the segment (3). Each channel is mean-centered, and quiet lead-in and lead-out frames are trimmed.
38	    37	3. **Matching** (`DTW`, `TemplateClassifier`). Each channel is z-scaled across the training set. Matching is 1-nearest-neighbour per word, using dynamic time warping with a Sakoe–Chiba band. A segment is rejected if the best distance is above *max distance* or the margin to the runner-up is below *min confidence*.
39	    38	4. **Is it real?** (`Evaluation`). The leave-one-out accuracy is compared with the same procedure run on shuffled labels. If p < 0.05, the motion stream distinguishes your words better than chance.
40	    39	
41	    40	## Experiment protocol
42	    41	
43	    42	Use **Record Session** in the toolbar or on the Sensors screen. Recordings go to `~/Documents/Subvox/Sessions/<timestamp>-<condition>/`:
44	    43	
45	    44	- `motion.csv`: every motion sample. `t` is seconds from session start.
46	    45	- `audio.caf`: microphone audio, if the mic is running.
47	    46	- `events.csv`: every Space-held segment, with its label or prediction.
48	    47	- `meta.json`: condition, prompt, and the audio start offset for aligning audio with motion.
49	    48	
50	    49	Suggested runs: the same 5-word script under **Normal speech**, **Whisper** and **Silent mouthing**, 10 reps each. Then, in Train, compare the Evaluate results across feature sets.
51	    50	
52	    51	The training set lives at `~/Library/Application Support/Subvox/dataset.json`.
53	    52	
54	    53	## Known limits
55	    54	
56	    55	- Headphone motion is processed and low-rate (roughly 25 Hz on AirPods). The speech-detecting accelerometer and the inward mic are not exposed. Expect jaw and head movement, not vocal vibration.
57	    56	- Templates are user- and session-specific. Re-seating the AirPods can shift the signal.
58	    57	- Choosing AirPods as the mic input switches them to the Bluetooth headset (HFP) profile.

394	     1	import Foundation

396	     3	/// Dynamic time warping between two multichannel sequences, with a Sakoe–Chiba band.
397	     4	/// Lets the same mouthed word match when said faster or slower.
398	     5	enum DTW {
399	     6	    static func distance(_ a: [[Double]], _ b: [[Double]], bandFraction: Double = 0.25) -> Double {
400	     7	        let n = a.count, m = b.count
401	     8	        guard n > 0, m > 0 else { return .infinity }
402	     9	        let band = max(abs(n - m), Int(Double(max(n, m)) * bandFraction))
403	    10	
404	    11	        var previous = [Double](repeating: .infinity, count: m + 1)
405	    12	        var current = previous
406	    13	        previous[0] = 0
407	    14	
408	    15	        for i in 1...n {
409	    16	            for j in current.indices { current[j] = .infinity }
410	    17	            let lo = max(1, i - band)
411	    18	            let hi = min(m, i + band)
412	    19	            if lo <= hi {
413	    20	                for j in lo...hi {
414	    21	                    let cost = euclidean(a[i - 1], b[j - 1])
415	    22	                    current[j] = cost + min(previous[j], current[j - 1], previous[j - 1])
416	    23	                }
417	    24	            }
418	    25	            swap(&previous, &current)
419	    26	        }
420	    27	        // Normalize by the maximum path length so long and short words compare fairly.
421	    28	        return previous[m] / Double(n + m)
422	    29	    }
423	    30	
424	    31	    private static func euclidean(_ x: [Double], _ y: [Double]) -> Double {
425	    32	        var sum = 0.0
426	    33	        for k in 0..<min(x.count, y.count) {
427	    34	            let d = x[k] - y[k]
428	    35	            sum += d * d
429	    36	        }
430	    37	        return sum.squareRoot()
431	    38	    }
432	    39	}

436	     3	/// Which motion channels feed the classifier. Toggling these is the ablation experiment:

438	     5	struct FeatureSet: OptionSet, Codable, Hashable, Sendable {
439	     6	    let rawValue: Int
440	     7	
441	     8	    static let acceleration = FeatureSet(rawValue: 1 << 0)
442	     9	    static let rotation = FeatureSet(rawValue: 1 << 1)
443	    10	    static let attitude = FeatureSet(rawValue: 1 << 2)

447	    14	enum MotionFeatures {
448	    15	    /// Activity score used for segmentation. Rotation (rad/s) and acceleration (g) live on
449	    16	    /// different scales; the 5× weight puts typical jaw-motion values in the same range.
450	    17	    static func energy(_ s: MotionSample) -> Double {
451	    18	        let rotation = (s.rx * s.rx + s.ry * s.ry + s.rz * s.rz).squareRoot()
452	    19	        let accel = (s.ax * s.ax + s.ay * s.ay + s.az * s.az).squareRoot()
453	    20	        return rotation + 5 * accel
454	    21	    }
455	    22	
456	    23	    /// Drops quiet lead-in/lead-out frames so templates align on the articulation itself.
457	    24	    /// Uses a threshold relative to the segment so it behaves the same for training and decoding.
458	    25	    static func trim(_ samples: [MotionSample], padding: Int = 2) -> [MotionSample] {
459	    26	        guard samples.count > 6 else { return samples }
460	    27	        let energies = samples.map(energy)
461	    28	        let sorted = energies.sorted()
462	    29	        let floor = sorted[sorted.count / 5]
463	    30	        let peak = sorted[sorted.count - 1]
464	    31	        guard peak > floor * 1.5 else { return samples }
465	    32	        let threshold = floor + 0.15 * (peak - floor)
466	    33	        guard let first = energies.firstIndex(where: { $0 > threshold }),
467	    34	              let last = energies.lastIndex(where: { $0 > threshold }) else { return samples }
468	    35	        let lo = max(0, first - padding)
469	    36	        let hi = min(samples.count - 1, last + padding)
470	    37	        guard hi - lo + 1 >= 5 else { return samples }
471	    38	        return Array(samples[lo...hi])

=== README.md
     1	# Subvox
     2	
     3	A macOS prototype that tests whether AirPods Pro head-motion data (`CMHeadphoneMotionManager`) carries enough information to turn **silently mouthed words into text**.
     4	
     5	It doesn't use a language model. It's a small-vocabulary template recognizer plus a statistical test that tells you whether the signal is real.
     6	
     7	## Build & run
     8	
     9	```sh
    10	brew install xcodegen   # once
    11	xcodegen generate
    12	open Subvox.xcodeproj   # ⌘R
    13	```
    14	
    15	Or from the command line:
    16	
    17	```sh
    18	xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build -allowProvisioningUpdates build
    19	open build/Build/Products/Debug/Subvox.app
    20	xcodebuild -project Subvox.xcodeproj -scheme Subvox -derivedDataPath build test
    21	```
    22	
    23	Requires macOS 14+, AirPods Pro or another headphone that supports head tracking, connected as the Mac's audio output. On first launch, grant **Motion**. The mic and speech prompts only appear when you start the mic.
    24	
    25	## Screens
    26	
    27	| Screen | What it does |
    28	|---|---|
    29	| **Sensors** | Live plots of user acceleration, rotation rate and attitude, the measured sample rate, a mic input picker and level meter, and a recorder for experiment sessions. |
    30	| **Train** | Pick a word, hold **Space**, mouth it, release. Each take is stored as a template. **Evaluate** runs leave-one-out classification and a 500× label-permutation test, then shows accuracy against chance, a p-value and a confusion matrix. The feature checkboxes (acceleration / rotation / attitude) let you test which channels carry the signal. |
    31	| **Decode** | The motion-to-text screen. Hold Space, or use auto-detect after calibrating the noise floor. Each segment is DTW-matched against your templates and added to the transcript. A live mic transcript runs alongside it for comparison. |
    32	
    33	## How decoding works
    34	
    35	1. **Segmentation** (`CaptureController`). Space-hold, or an energy trigger above a calibrated noise floor with pre-roll and hangover.
    36	2. **Features** (`MotionFeatures`). Per frame: user acceleration (3), rotation rate (3), and attitude change since the start of the segment (3). Each channel is mean-centered, and quiet lead-in and lead-out frames are trimmed.
    37	3. **Matching** (`DTW`, `TemplateClassifier`). Each channel is z-scaled across the training set. Matching is 1-nearest-neighbour per word, using dynamic time warping with a Sakoe–Chiba band. A segment is rejected if the best distance is above *max distance* or the margin to the runner-up is below *min confidence*.
    38	4. **Is it real?** (`Evaluation`). The leave-one-out accuracy is compared with the same procedure run on shuffled labels. If p < 0.05, the motion stream distinguishes your words better than chance.
    39	
    40	## Experiment protocol
    41	
    42	Use **Record Session** in the toolbar or on the Sensors screen. Recordings go to `~/Documents/Subvox/Sessions/<timestamp>-<condition>/`:
    43	
    44	- `motion.csv`: every motion sample. `t` is seconds from session start.
    45	- `audio.caf`: microphone audio, if the mic is running.
    46	- `events.csv`: every Space-held segment, with its label or prediction.
    47	- `meta.json`: condition, prompt, and the audio start offset for aligning audio with motion.
    48	
    49	Suggested runs: the same 5-word script under **Normal speech**, **Whisper** and **Silent mouthing**, 10 reps each. Then, in Train, compare the Evaluate results across feature sets.
    50	
    51	The training set lives at `~/Library/Application Support/Subvox/dataset.json`.
    52	
    53	## Known limits
    54	
    55	- Headphone motion is processed and low-rate (roughly 25 Hz on AirPods). The speech-detecting accelerometer and the inward mic are not exposed. Expect jaw and head movement, not vocal vibration.
    56	- Templates are user- and session-specific. Re-seating the AirPods can shift the signal.
    57	- Choosing AirPods as the mic input switches them to the Bluetooth headset (HFP) profile.

     1	import CoreMotion
     2	import Observation
     3	
     4	/// Streams `CMHeadphoneMotionManager` updates from connected AirPods.
     5	@MainActor @Observable
     6	final class HeadphoneMotionService {
     7	    enum Status: Equatable {
     8	        case unsupported
     9	        case denied
    10	        case waiting
    11	        case streaming
    12	        case error(String)
    13	
    14	        var label: String {
    15	            switch self {
    16	            case .unsupported: "Headphone motion unsupported"
    17	            case .denied: "Motion access denied"
    18	            case .waiting: "Waiting for AirPods"
    19	            case .streaming: "Streaming"
    20	            case .error(let message): message
    21	            }
    22	        }
    23	    }
    24	
    25	    static let historySeconds: TimeInterval = 10
    26	
    27	    private(set) var status: Status = .waiting
    28	    private(set) var isConnected = false
    29	    private(set) var latest: MotionSample?
    30	    private(set) var history: [MotionSample] = []
    31	    private(set) var sampleRate: Double = 0
    32	    private(set) var sampleCount = 0
    33	
    34	    var onSample: ((MotionSample) -> Void)?
    35	
    36	    @ObservationIgnored private let manager = CMHeadphoneMotionManager()
    37	    @ObservationIgnored private let proxy = DelegateProxy()
    38	    @ObservationIgnored private var rateWindow: [TimeInterval] = []
    39	
    40	    func start() {
    41	        guard manager.isDeviceMotionAvailable else {
    42	            status = .unsupported
    43	            return
    44	        }
    45	        switch CMHeadphoneMotionManager.authorizationStatus() {
    46	        case .denied, .restricted:
    47	            status = .denied
    48	            return
    49	        default:
    50	            break
    51	        }
    52	
    53	        proxy.onChange = { [weak self] connected in
    54	            Task { @MainActor in self?.connectionChanged(connected) }
    55	        }
    56	        manager.delegate = proxy
    57	        manager.startConnectionStatusUpdates()
    58	        manager.startDeviceMotionUpdates(to: .main) { [weak self] motion, error in
    59	            MainActor.assumeIsolated {
    60	                self?.handle(motion, error)
    61	            }
    62	        }
    63	    }
    64	
    65	    func stop() {
    66	        manager.stopDeviceMotionUpdates()
    67	        manager.stopConnectionStatusUpdates()
    68	    }
    69	
    70	    private func connectionChanged(_ connected: Bool) {
    71	        isConnected = connected
    72	        if !connected {
    73	            status = .waiting
    74	            sampleRate = 0
    75	            rateWindow.removeAll()
    76	        }
    77	    }
    78	
    79	    private func handle(_ motion: CMDeviceMotion?, _ error: Error?) {
    80	        if let error {
    81	            let ns = error as NSError
    82	            if ns.domain == CMErrorDomain, ns.code == Int(CMErrorMotionActivityNotAuthorized.rawValue) {
    83	                status = .denied
    84	            } else {
    85	                status = .error(error.localizedDescription)
    86	            }
    87	            return
    88	        }
    89	        guard let motion else { return }
    90	
    91	        let sample = MotionSample(motion)
    92	        latest = sample
    93	        status = .streaming
    94	        isConnected = true
    95	        sampleCount += 1
    96	
    97	        history.append(sample)
    98	        let cutoff = sample.t - Self.historySeconds
    99	        if let firstKept = history.firstIndex(where: { $0.t >= cutoff }), firstKept > 0 {
   100	            history.removeFirst(firstKept)
   101	        }
   102	
   103	        rateWindow.append(sample.t)
   104	        rateWindow.removeAll { $0 < sample.t - 1 }
   105	        if let first = rateWindow.first, sample.t > first {
   106	            sampleRate = Double(rateWindow.count - 1) / (sample.t - first)
   107	        }
   108	
   109	        onSample?(sample)
   110	    }
   111	}

   116	    func headphoneMotionManagerDidConnect(_ manager: CMHeadphoneMotionManager) {

   118	    }
   119

   121	        onChange?(false)

=== Subvox/Decoding/DTW.swift
     1	import Foundation
     2	
     3	/// Dynamic time warping between two multichannel sequences, with a Sakoe–Chiba band.
     4	/// Lets the same mouthed word match when said faster or slower.
     5	enum DTW {
     6	    static func distance(_ a: [[Double]], _ b: [[Double]], bandFraction: Double = 0.25) -> Double {
     7	        let n = a.count, m = b.count
     8	        guard n > 0, m > 0 else { return .infinity }
     9	        let band = max(abs(n - m), Int(Double(max(n, m)) * bandFraction))
    10	
    11	        var previous = [Double](repeating: .infinity, count: m + 1)
    12	        var current = previous
    13	        previous[0] = 0
    14	
    15	        for i in 1...n {
    16	            for j in current.indices { current[j] = .infinity }
    17	            let lo = max(1, i - band)
    18	            let hi = min(m, i + band)
    19	            if lo <= hi {
    20	                for j in lo...hi {
    21	                    let cost = euclidean(a[i - 1], b[j - 1])
    22	                    current[j] = cost + min(previous[j], current[j - 1], previous[j - 1])
    23	                }
    24	            }
    25	            swap(&previous, &current)
    26	        }
    27	        // Normalize by the maximum path length so long and short words compare fairly.
    28	        return previous[m] / Double(n + m)
    29	    }
    30	
    31	    private static func euclidean(_ x: [Double], _ y: [Double]) -> Double {
    32	        var sum = 0.0
    33	        for k in 0..<min(x.count, y.count) {
    34	            let d = x[k] - y[k]
    35	            sum += d * d
    36	        }
    37	        return sum.squareRoot()
    38	    }
    39	}

     1	import Foundation
     2	
     3	/// Which motion channels feed the classifier. Toggling these is the ablation experiment:
     4	/// does articulation show up in acceleration, rotation, or slow head attitude?
     5	struct FeatureSet: OptionSet, Codable, Hashable, Sendable {
     6	    let rawValue: Int
     7	
     8	    static let acceleration = FeatureSet(rawValue: 1 << 0)
     9	    static let rotation = FeatureSet(rawValue: 1 << 1)
    10	    static let attitude = FeatureSet(rawValue: 1 << 2)
    11	    static let all: FeatureSet = [.acceleration, .rotation, .attitude]
    12	}
    13	
    14	enum MotionFeatures {
    15	    /// Activity score used for segmentation. Rotation (rad/s) and acceleration (g) live on
    16	    /// different scales; the 5× weight puts typical jaw-motion values in the same range.
    17	    static func energy(_ s: MotionSample) -> Double {
    18	        let rotation = (s.rx * s.rx + s.ry * s.ry + s.rz * s.rz).squareRoot()
    19	        let accel = (s.ax * s.ax + s.ay * s.ay + s.az * s.az).squareRoot()
    20	        return rotation + 5 * accel
    21	    }
    22	
    23	    /// Drops quiet lead-in/lead-out frames so templates align on the articulation itself.
    24	    /// Uses a threshold relative to the segment so it behaves the same for training and decoding.
    25	    static func trim(_ samples: [MotionSample], padding: Int = 2) -> [MotionSample] {
    26	        guard samples.count > 6 else { return samples }
    27	        let energies = samples.map(energy)
    28	        let sorted = energies.sorted()
    29	        let floor = sorted[sorted.count / 5]
    30	        let peak = sorted[sorted.count - 1]
    31	        guard peak > floor * 1.5 else { return samples }
    32	        let threshold = floor + 0.15 * (peak - floor)
    33	        guard let first = energies.firstIndex(where: { $0 > threshold }),
    34	              let last = energies.lastIndex(where: { $0 > threshold }) else { return samples }
    35	        let lo = max(0, first - padding)
    36	        let hi = min(samples.count - 1, last + padding)
    37	        guard hi - lo + 1 >= 5 else { return samples }
    38	        return Array(samples[lo...hi])
    39	    }
    40	
    41	    /// Per-frame feature vectors, mean-centered per channel (removes posture/heading bias).
    42	    static func frames(_ samples: [MotionSample], set: FeatureSet) -> [[Double]] {
    43	        guard let origin = samples.first else { return [] }
    44	        var frames = samples.map { s -> [Double] in
    45	            var v: [Double] = []
    46	            if set.contains(.acceleration) { v += [s.ax, s.ay, s.az] }
    47	            if set.contains(.rotation) { v += [s.rx, s.ry, s.rz] }
    48	            if set.contains(.attitude) {
    49	                v += [wrapped(s.pitch - origin.pitch), wrapped(s.roll - origin.roll), wrapped(s.yaw - origin.yaw)]
    50	            }
    51	            return v
    52	        }
    53	        guard let dims = frames.first?.count, dims > 0 else { return frames }
    54	        for d in 0..<dims {

    30	/// Small-vocabulary recognizer: nearest-neighbour DTW against user-recorded templates.
    31	/// Deliberately simple — the question this prototype answers is whether the signal is
    32	/// there at all, not how far a big model can push it.
    33	struct TemplateClassifier: Sendable {
    34	    let featureSet: FeatureSet
    35	    private let entries: [(label: String, frames: [[Double]])]
    36	    private let scales: [Double]
    37	
    38	    var labels: [String] { Array(Set(entries.map(\.label))).sorted() }
    39	
    40	    init?(templates: [Template], featureSet: FeatureSet) {
    41	        guard !featureSet.isEmpty else { return nil }
    42	        let raw = templates.map { MotionFeatures.frames(MotionFeatures.trim($0.samples), set: featureSet) }
    43	        guard Set(templates.map(\.label)).count >= 2 else { return nil }
    44	        let scales = MotionFeatures.channelScales(raw)
    45	        self.featureSet = featureSet
    46	        self.scales = scales
    47	        self.entries = zip(templates, raw).map { ($0.label, MotionFeatures.scaled($1, by: scales)) }
    48	    }
    49	
    50	    func rank(_ samples: [MotionSample]) -> [RankedLabel] {
    51	        let query = MotionFeatures.scaled(
    52	            MotionFeatures.frames(MotionFeatures.trim(samples), set: featureSet), by: scales)
    53	        var best: [String: Double] = [:]
    54	        for entry in entries {
    55	            let d = DTW.distance(query, entry.frames)
    56	            best[entry.label] = min(best[entry.label] ?? .infinity, d)
    57	        }
    58	        return best.map { RankedLabel(label: $0.key, distance: $0.value) }.sorted { $0.distance < $1.distance }
    59	    }

    61	    func predict(_ samples: [MotionSample], maxDistance: Double, minConfidence: Double) -> Prediction {
    62	        let ranked = rank(samples)
    63	        let confidence = Self.margin(ranked.map(\.distance))
    64	        let accepted = (ranked.first?.distance ?? .infinity) <= maxDistance && confidence >= minConfidence

    66	    }

    68	    static func margin(_ sortedDistances: [Double]) -> Double {
    69	        guard sortedDistances.count >= 2, sortedDistances[1] > 0 else { return 0 }
    70	        return max(0, 1 - sortedDistances[0] / sortedDistances[1])
    71	    }

    74	/// Leave-one-out accuracy plus a label-permutation test: the honest answer to
    75	/// "is the motion stream statistically distinguishable between words?"
    76	struct Evaluation: Sendable {
    77	    var labels: [String]
    78	    /// confusion[actual][predicted]
    79	    var confusion: [[Int]]
    80	    var accuracy: Double
    81	    /// Accuracy of always guessing the most common label.
    82	    var chance: Double
    83	    var permutationMean: Double
    84	    var permutationP95: Double
    85	    var pValue: Double

    88	
    89	    static func run(templates: [Template], featureSet: FeatureSet, permutations: Int = 500) -> Evaluation? {
    90	        let labels = Array(Set(templates.map(\.label))).sorted()
    91	        let counts = Dictionary(grouping: templates, by: \.label).mapValues(\.count)
    92	        guard labels.count >= 2, counts.values.allSatisfy({ $0 >= 2 }), !featureSet.isEmpty else { return nil }
    93	
    94	        let raw = templates.map { MotionFeatures.frames(MotionFeatures.trim($0.samples), set: featureSet) }
    95	        let scales = MotionFeatures.channelScales(raw)
    96	        let seqs = raw.map { MotionFeatures.scaled($0, by: scales) }
    97	        let n = seqs.count
    98	
    99	        // Pairwise distances once; every labelling (true or permuted) reuses them.
   100	        var distance = [[Double]](repeating: [Double](repeating: 0, count: n), count: n)
   101	        for i in 0..<n {
   102	            for j in (i + 1)..<max(i + 1, n) {
   103	                let d = DTW.distance(seqs[i], seqs[j])
   104	                distance[i][j] = d
   105	                distance[j][i] = d
   106	            }
   107	        }
   108	
   109	        let index = Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: labels.enumerated().map { ($1, $0) })
   110	        let truth = templates.map { index[$0.label]! }
   111	
   112	        func leaveOneOut(_ assignment: [Int]) -> [Int] {
   113	            (0..<n).map { i in
   114	                var best = [Double](repeating: .infinity, count: labels.count)
   115	                for j in 0..<n where j != i {
   116	                    best[assignment[j]] = min(best[assignment[j]], distance[i][j])
   117	                }
   118	                return best.indices.min { best[$0] < best[$1] }!
   119	            }
   120	        }
   121	
   122	        func accuracy(_ predicted: [Int], _ actual: [Int]) -> Double {
   123	            Double(zip(predicted, actual).filter { $0 == $1 }.count) / Double(n)
   124	        }
   125	
   126	        let predicted = leaveOneOut(truth)
   127	        var confusion = [[Int]](repeating: [Int](repeating: 0, count: labels.count), count: labels.count)
   128	        for (p, a) in zip(predicted, truth) { confusion[a][p] += 1 }
   129	        let observed = accuracy(predicted, truth)
   130	
   131	        var generator = SystemRandomNumberGenerator()
   132	        var nullAccuracies: [Double] = []
   133	        nullAccuracies.reserveCapacity(permutations)
   134	        for _ in 0..<permutations {
   135	            let shuffled = truth.shuffled(using: &generator)
   136	            nullAccuracies.append(accuracy(leaveOneOut(shuffled), shuffled))
   137	        }
   138	        nullAccuracies.sort()
   139	        let atLeast = nullAccuracies.filter { $0 >= observed }.count
   140	
   141	        return Evaluation(
   142	            labels: labels,
   143	            confusion: confusion,
   144	            accuracy: observed,
   145	            chance: Double(counts.values.max()!) / Double(n),
   146	            permutationMean: nullAccuracies.reduce(0, +) / Double(max(permutations, 1)),
   147	            permutationP95: nullAccuracies.isEmpty ? 0 : nullAccuracies[Int(Double(nullAccuracies.count - 1) * 0.95)],
   148	            pValue: Double(atLeast + 1) / Double(permutations + 1),
   149	            permutations: permutations,
   150	            templateCount: n)
   151	    }
   152	}

    33	        var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<AudioDeviceID>.size)

    41	            mScope: kAudioObjectPropertyScopeGlobal,
    42	            mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain)
    43	        var name: Unmanaged<CFString>?
    44	        var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<Unmanaged<CFString>?>.size)
    45	        let status = withUnsafeMutablePointer(to: &name) {
    46	            AudioObjectGetPropertyData(id, &address, 0, nil, &size, $0)
    47	        }

    55	            mScope: kAudioDevicePropertyScopeInput,
    56	            mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain)

    58	        guard AudioObjectGetPropertyDataSize(id, &address, 0, nil, &size) == noErr, size > 0 else { return 0 }

     5	/// Fans microphone buffers out to consumers (speech recognizer, session recorder) on the
     6	/// audio render thread. Consumers must be cheap and thread-safe.
     7	final class AudioSink: @unchecked Sendable {
     8	    typealias Consumer = (AVAudioPCMBuffer, AVAudioTime) -> Void
     9	
    10	    private let lock = NSLock()
    11	    private var consumers: [UUID: Consumer] = [:]
    12	    private var onLevel: ((Float) -> Void)?
    13	
    14	    func add(_ consumer: @escaping Consumer) -> UUID {
    15	        let id = UUID()
    16	        lock.withLock { consumers[id] = consumer }
    17	        return id
    18	    }
    19	
    20	    func remove(_ id: UUID) {
    21	        lock.withLock { _ = consumers.removeValue(forKey: id) }
    22	    }
    23	
    24	    func setLevelHandler(_ handler: ((Float) -> Void)?) {
    25	        lock.withLock { onLevel = handler }
    26	    }
    27	
    28	    func dispatch(_ buffer: AVAudioPCMBuffer, _ time: AVAudioTime) {
    29	        let (current, levelHandler) = lock.withLock { (Array(consumers.values), onLevel) }
    30	        for consumer in current { consumer(buffer, time) }
    31	        levelHandler?(Self.normalizedLevel(buffer))
    32	    }
    33	
    34	    /// RMS of channel 0 mapped from -60…0 dBFS onto 0…1.
    35	    private static func normalizedLevel(_ buffer: AVAudioPCMBuffer) -> Float {
    36	        guard let samples = buffer.floatChannelData?[0], buffer.frameLength > 0 else { return 0 }
    37	        let n = Int(buffer.frameLength)
    38	        var sum: Float = 0
    39	        for i in 0..<n { sum += samples[i] * samples[i] }
    40	        let rms = (sum / Float(n)).squareRoot()
    41	        let db = 20 * log10(max(rms, 1e-7))
    42	        return max(0, min(1, (db + 60) / 60))
    43	    }
    44	}

content.text:
I read all of subvox, which is MIT-licensed. Its pipeline is: about 25 Hz of processed AirPods head motion → energy-based segmentation → 9 features (acceleration, rotation, attitude change) → nearest-template matching that allows for different speaking speeds → a statistical check that the results beat chance.

The overall design is sound. It keeps the raw samples, so every idea below can be tested on data you've already recorded. Because the signal is weak and slow, the gains will mostly come from cleaner features, a better classifier and much more labelled data, not from making the code faster.

## Accuracy (highest impact first)

1. **Put samples on an even time grid.** `MotionFeatures.frames` treats each sample as one frame, but Bluetooth delivery jitters and drops samples. Spacing them evenly at 25 Hz using the timestamps (`t`) stops a gap from looking like the word was said faster.
2. **Filter out head movement.** Jaw motion sits roughly in the 1.5–8 Hz range, and 12.5 Hz is the ceiling at 25 Hz. Nods, posture shifts and attitude drift are slower. Filtering below about 1 Hz and adding rate-of-change features should help more than anything else, especially for the attitude channels.
3. **Simulate re-seating during training.** The README says re-seating the AirPods shifts the signal; a re-seat is essentially a small rotation of the sensor axes. Adding training copies that are randomly rotated by ±10–15°, with small time-stretch and scale changes, attacks that problem directly. It also multiplies each real take into many.
4. **Add a "not a word" class.** Record swallowing, chewing, head turns, smiling and talking normally as a `_none` label. Right now rejection relies on hand-tuned limits (`maxDistance`, and `minConfidence`, which is `1 − d1/d2`). An explicit noise class is much more reliable, and auto-detect needs it.
5. **Use a better classifier than a single nearest match.** Matching only the single closest recording is fragile when one take is bad. In rough order of effort:
   - Vote across the few closest matches, or compare against averaged per-word templates (DBA).
   - Weight each sensor channel by how well it separates words.
   - Try MiniRocket with a ridge classifier. It's the strongest known method for small time-series datasets, trains in seconds on a CPU and is easy to port to Swift.
   - Create ML's Activity Classifier is a no-code baseline built for exactly this kind of motion data.
6. **Record which earbud the data came from.** `CMDeviceMotion.sensorLocation` reports left or right, and the stream can switch between earbuds. Templates from different ears shouldn't be mixed silently.
7. **Choose words the sensor can tell apart.** At 25 Hz it sees how wide the jaw opens and how many syllables there are, not the tongue or lips. Use the confusion matrix to pick words with distinct jaw shapes, for example one versus three syllables, or open versus closed vowels.

## Make the accuracy numbers trustworthy

- **The current evaluation overstates accuracy.** It holds out one take at a time, but takes recorded back to back are nearly identical. Hold out whole sessions or re-seats instead.
- **A small leak inflates the score.** In the evaluation, `channelScales` is computed with the held-out take included.

Without these two fixes you can't tell which of the improvements above actually work.

## Training and data collection

- **Label data automatically with the mic.** Speak or whisper while recording motion, and Apple's speech recognizer timestamps each word, which gives you labelled motion segments for free. Use the Mac's built-in mic for this. Choosing the AirPods mic switches them to the lower-quality headset profile. This data is close to, but not the same as, silent mouthing, so use it to pretrain or start the model, then fine-tune on a small silent set.
- **Run prompted sessions.** Show the words in random order with a beep through the AirPods, advance automatically, and build in a re-seat every N takes. That removes the manual Space-bar labelling and the order effects.
- **Ask for more takes where it's weakest.** After each evaluation, request extra takes for the most-confused word pairs.
- **Keep learning while you use it.** Add decoded words you confirm back into the training set.

## Speed

Speed isn't a real problem at this scale: a 2 s word is about 50 frames, so matching against 100 templates is trivial. The perceived lag comes from the 0.35 s silence wait in `CaptureController` plus Bluetooth delay. Worthwhile anyway:

- Deliver motion updates on their own queue instead of `.main`, so UI redraws can't delay them.
- Move `predict` off the main thread.
- Add a fast pre-check (LB_Keogh) that skips most full comparisons once the vocabulary grows.
- Stop rewriting the whole JSON dataset after every take.

## Hard limits with AirPods Pro 2 only

- You only get the processed motion stream at about 25 Hz.
- Apps can't reach the voice-detecting accelerometer or the inward-facing mic.

<preview_tools>
To run and verify this project's dev server, use preview_start `{name: "…"}`: it starts the named dev server from .claude/launch.json and opens a tab at its localhost port. Never use Bash to run dev servers. The result includes a `tabId` — pass it to read_page / computer / navigate / etc. to target that tab. `tabs_context` lists every open tab; omitting tabId acts on the fronted tab. `serverId` in the result is the PROCESS id, used only for preview_stop and preview_logs.

<when_to_verify>
Run the verification workflow only when the change would be observable in the browser preview — something the dev server renders, serves, or logs. If the change affects code the preview can't exercise (a different runtime, tests, types, tooling, or work that isn't ready to run yet), skip verification — don't start a server that won't prove anything.
</when_to_verify>

<verification_workflow>
After editing code that is previewable, verify it works. Never ask the user to check manually — verify and share proof directly.

1. Ensure a preview is open: preview_start with `{name}` for the dev server (or `{url}` for an external site).
2. Reload if needed (navigate to the current URL again, or javascript_tool: window.location.reload()). Skip if HMR is active.

Check for issues using text-based tools:
3. read_console_messages, preview_logs, or read_network_requests for errors.
4. read_page for content and structure (returns refs you can pass to computer/form_input).
5. javascript_tool for computed CSS values.
6. computer (click/type) or form_input to test interactions, then read_page to confirm.
7. resize_window for responsive or dark mode.

If issues are found, read source code to diagnose, edit source files to fix, then re-check from step 3. Use javascript_tool for debugging only.

Once everything is working, share proof with the user:
8. computer {action: "screenshot"} for visual changes, read_network_requests for API changes, or preview_logs for server changes.

Skip steps that aren't relevant — e.g. skip step 5 for non-CSS changes, skip step 7 unless layout or theming changed.
</verification_workflow>
</preview_tools>

<simulator_tools>
When the user wants to run, test, or visually check an iOS app ("run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?"), use mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control. Simulators and emulators only — when the user asks to run on their physical device ("on my phone", "on my device"), build for the device with your normal build tools instead; these tools and the panel cannot drive a real device. Open the live panel ('attach') whenever the user would want to see the app themselves — and call 'attach' FIRST, before you build or launch: it is cheap, it opens instantly on a booted device (and surfaces the one-time device-access prompt while the user is still at the keyboard), and if nothing is booted it returns a harmless, clear error — boot or build first in that case, then attach as soon as a device is up. Do not defer the panel to the implicit re-attach in 'launch'; the panel should already be open while you build. The panel is the user's view; your own verification (screenshot, tap, text) is headless and works without it — verify yourself rather than asking the user to check. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. If 'attach' fails, follow the error's remediation: address the cause (for example no booted device, or device access not granted) or tell the user — don't retry the same call in a loop unless the error says retrying will work. If the failure is the host's Xcode setup (a wrong xcode-select, missing Xcode, or a missing iOS platform), tell the user right away with the exact fix the error gives — most of these fixes need their password, so you cannot run them (the error itself says when a fix is one you can run) — and if you continue by driving the Simulator app with generic screen tools instead, say so explicitly; never switch silently. An app in the iOS Simulator reaches a server on the machine your shell runs on at localhost, with no port forwarding.
</simulator_tools>

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it.
